beats.lead: The most famous experiment never actually run
beats.text: Schrodinger did not believe his cat was really alive and dead at once.
beats.note: He built the scenario to make that idea sound ridiculous, not to describe something he thought was true.

beats.name: Erwin Schrodinger
beats.role: Published the thought experiment in the journal Naturwissenschaften, responding to Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen's paper on quantum theory from earlier that year.

beats.text: In the scenario, a sealed box holds a cat alongside a radioactive atom with a fifty percent chance of triggering poison.
beats.note: Quantum mechanics, applied literally to the whole box, says the cat is neither alive nor dead until someone looks: a blend of both at once.

beats.text: Schrodinger was arguing that this was absurd, and that something was wrong with treating a cat by the same quantum rules as a single atom.
beats.note: The Copenhagen interpretation he was criticising is still the one most commonly taught today.

beats.text: The joke became the textbook example of the thing it was mocking.

beats.line: He built it to sound absurd. It became the icon.
